events.title: Tòmas Odhar's hand on the gatepost
events.body: At the fallen gate of the Muileann chrom store the old hewer Tòmas Odhar rests his hand flat on the gatepost and says he has carried coal out through it for six-and-thirty years and never thought to see rifles carried out through it instead. His words are repeated round the camp for a week after.

events.title: Mòrag takes the sergeant's rifle herself
events.body: Mòrag nic Iain Maor lifts the surrendered sergeant's rifle from the cobbles of the Muileann chrom store with her own hand rather than leave it to be gathered by another, the first weapon she has carried since she broke the overseer's staff the summer before.

events.title: Pàdraig Reamhar scuttles his own barge
events.body: The boatman Pàdraig Reamhar, who built the larger of the two barges sunk at Ceann fhada with his own father twenty years before, knocks the plugs from her hull with his own hands and says afterward only that she had been a good boat.

events.title: Oswin Frayne rowed out from Ceann fhada
events.body: A' Chompanaidh's harbour-master at Ceann fhada, Oswin Frayne, is rowed out past his own sunk barges and set aboard a boat for any harbour still flying Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's flag, unharmed, on the crews' own order.

events.title: Bread goes to the half-loaf at Baile thais
events.body: By the seventh day of the siege of the walled store, the camp at Baile thais cuts its bread to a half-loaf a household, and the children who had at first jeered at the wall grow quiet and keep to their mothers' fires.

events.title: The constables of Baile thais sent to the coast
events.body: On Eilidh nic Raghnaill's written order, carried down from Comhairle na Coille by a girl of fourteen, Seumas Ciar sends the thirty-one constables who yield the Baile thais store to the coast whole and fed, over the objection of hewers who have buried kin to the same walls.

events.title: Uilleam Gobha's first grenades tried
events.body: On a moonless night behind his forge at Muileann dhearg, Uilleam Gobha tries the first of his tin-cased grenades, with only his eldest son holding a lamp a safe way off, and says it will do.

events.title: A finger lost before Uilleam Gobha's care
events.body: Before Uilleam Gobha takes up the crimping of the powder tins himself, another smith of Muileann dhearg loses three fingers to the work, a loss Uilleam afterward says he was determined it would not cost him.

events.title: The council-hall lock broken with a coal-hammer
events.body: The custodians of Cathair dhearg break Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's locks on their own council-hall doors with a coal-hammer borrowed from the smithy across the square, and sit down again in the chairs shut from them for two years.

events.title: The coal-carts turned on their sides
events.body: The townsfolk of Cathair dhearg barricade the coal-cart bridge with A' Chompanaidh's own carts, turned on their sides and lashed together with ironmonger's chain, and hold it three days until the constables sent against it are called back to the harbour.

events.title: Strake's letter asking for a ship before winter
events.body: Lionel Strake writes to A' Chompanaidh's directors over the sea that the harbour town below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir holds itself apart from the fighting only until it judges which side will leave it better off, and asks for more men, powder and a ship before the northern passage closes.

events.title: The house swept at Baile thais
events.body: Constables sent under Strake's order find Eilidh nic Raghnaill's house at Baile thais standing open, its hearth three days cold, and the whole town silent around it, its people gone from door and window before the constables' captain can ask why.

events.title: The turnip cart to the ford
events.body: A cart with a false floor of turnips carries Uilleam Gobha's grenades up Rathad na Mèinne, past the cut, to the crews waiting at the ford of Àth chiar, the first of his work to leave Muileann dhearg for open fighting.

events.title: The nineteen of Àth chiar buried
events.body: The council's clerk Fionnuala writes down by lamp-light the names of the nineteen dead of Àth chiar and reads the list aloud the next morning; within the week they are buried on the moor above Cnoc naomh, within sight of the cairn raised there before the fighting began.

events.title: Dùghall counts the grain carts from Seann Warr
events.body: At the harbour quarter's upper gate Dùghall Dubh, once a weigher of coal for A' Chompanaidh, keeps the council's tally of the grain train down from Seann Warr, twelve carts against a capital's hunger, and sends the last load on to the sharing-yard behind the custodians' hall.

events.title: The sharing-yard of Cathair dhearg keeps an equal share
events.body: Through the siege the custodians of Cathair dhearg measure the city's grain out by household at a scale behind their hall, and take no more from it than any household waiting in the line before them, a fairness the city's own hunger remembers afterward better than any speech.

events.title: Dùghall puts the question to six men of the quarter
events.body: Asked by the council's captains whether the harbour quarter can reach A' Chompanaidh's counting-house without a shot fired, Dùghall Dubh puts the question first to six men born within sight of its roof, and all six answer that a fire lit quietly will hold Strake's men longer than a shot ever could.

events.title: The night clerk of the counting-house is taken without a blow
events.body: The counting-house's night clerk is found sitting on its steps in his shirt with his hands laced over his head before the raiders reach the ground floor, and Dùghall Dubh judges, from the look of him, that some part of the man had waited a year for the night to come.

events.title: Seven men cross the roofs in stocking feet
events.body: On a night of low cloud Dùghall Dubh and six men of the harbour quarter cross the net-loft roof-ridge to A' Chompanaidh's counting-house on hands and knees, in their stocking feet, and go down by rope through garret windows marked beforehand in daylight.

events.title: Word of the spared ledger refused reaches the harbour quarter
events.body: A rider from Ceann àrsaidh brings the harbour quarter word that the custodian there asked one tithe ledger be kept whole for the record, and that his own townsfolk, naming the danger of any debt kept on paper, carried it to the burning pile with the rest.

events.title: The camps set the burning of the ledgers to a verse
events.body: Before the ash of the Muileann chrom weigh-house has cooled, the camp folk are already singing eight words of it at market, and the verse travels the coast faster than any rider: they burned the book, but they did not burn the hill.

events.title: Fearchar Beag sights Blàr Cnoc ghorm
events.body: Sent up to the net-loft roof with a borrowed glass, Fearchar Beag reads Strake's last sally on the eastern road by its riderless horses coming back down alone, and brings the harbour quarter word by noon that the guns have gone quiet.

events.title: The captain of Muileann dhearg asks first for the wounded
events.body: When the harbour quarter's lower gates open, the council company's captain, a woman of Muileann dhearg unknown to Dùghall Dubh by name, thanks the gate-wardens and asks before anything else where the wounded of the counting-house alarm had been carried.

events.title: The letter-books found whole at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir
events.body: Where Strake has taken plate and account-papers down the river by night, Dùghall Dubh finds a room of Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books left standing untouched on an unlocked shelf, thirty years of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach's own correspondence with an Tìr Thall, and sends word of it to the council's clerks that evening.

events.title: Prentice the counting-house clerk goes down the river
events.body: Dùghall Dubh learns from a clerk taken at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir that Prentice, who weighed coal beside him nine years at the counting-house scales, went down the river with Strake's household the night Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir fell, leaving the ledgers he had kept behind as ash.

events.title: Clerks of the council begin to read Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's letter-books
events.body: By the morning after Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir falls, a table stands in its stripped hall with the first of the letter-books open under a lamp, and men who have never before read a stranger's hand bend over the close foreign script with the patience of a scale that will not balance.

events.title: Coinneach Beag puts his name forward
events.body: When the crew-leaders of the river towns ask for seven men who can keep their feet on a hill road and hold their tongues, Coinneach Beag, a boatman of Cuan dhearg raised on the river since boyhood and no stranger to A' Chompanaidh's rule over his own family, puts his name forward before he has properly decided to.

events.title: The letter read at a nameless hawk-house
events.body: On the road past Seann Toll, Coinneach Beag reads the council's letter aloud in a bare hawk-house of six benches, his voice unsteady at first; an old woman by the fire answers only that it has come to that, and no one else speaks.

events.title: The boy of Baile thais shows the wall
events.body: Passing through Baile thais, Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe is shown by a boy of nine or ten the marks on the store's outer wall from the siege's eleven days, told with more pride than fear, the town's memory of its own fight already settling into telling.

events.title: Word of Ashdown's retreat reaches Cuan dhearg
events.body: Through the fire's talk at Cuan dhearg the news of Ashdown's beaten column travels garbled and half-doubted: that Dùn chrom shut its gates on the soldiers who had slept a night in its barracks, and let the column go on to the coast without its own wounded, whom the town kept to nurse.

events.title: The seven wait nine hours at An Cupa Dàna
events.body: Seven men of the river towns gather at the inn of An Cupa Dàna and wait nine hours for the council's last letter, and in the waiting learn one another's names and fears: Coinneach Beag, Gillebrìde the hawk-priest's server, the coal-barge brothers, Ailig, and Pàdraig Buidhe, who says nothing at all.

events.title: The lead hawks given out
events.body: Each of the seven is given a small hawk cast in lead from cartridges taken at the store at Muileann chrom, worn at the throat on a cord of tarred twine as a token of the council's trust to whoever along the road might read it rightly.

events.title: The carter of Inis mhin
events.body: At Inis mhin, warned that Strake's constables now ride the western roads out of Ros bheag daily, the seven hire a carter with a covered cart and a mule, and leave the road for cart-tracks and field-edges known to no map, asking nothing of what he carries.

events.title: Eleven hours in the grass above Tobar dhomhain
events.body: Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe lies eleven hours in the long grass above the road from Ros bheag to the northern concession, counting every rider that passes; Gillebrìde keeps the tally on a strip of bark, a line for each rider and a cross for each leader.

events.title: Forty-one riders, all going south
events.body: The company's count ends at forty-one constables' riders in a single day, and not one riding north; Gillebrìde reads the sign as Strake's attention turned elsewhere, and Coinneach Beag cannot say whether the empty road is the safest on the island or the most dangerous.

events.title: The priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the letter
events.body: In the low temple above the harbour at Inis thais, the priests of Òrd na Cloiche hear the council's letter through in silence and will send no men, but shut the harbour to A' Chompanaidh's ships and open an Fhianna's own roads to the hawk-faithful.

events.title: The seven become one company
events.body: At the muster of the hawk-faithful under Ìomhar Seabhag at the western Seann Skell, the seven of Cuan dhearg stand in the company's first rank and are told they are one thing now, with one name: Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe.

events.title: Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill puts out her own light
events.body: At Tobar dhearg, Raonaid nic Dhòmhnaill, keeper of the light since her mother's death, climbs the tower alone on a night of her own choosing and puts out the beacon on her own authority, before any order from the council reaches her; the order finds the tower already dark.

events.title: Word of the burned coal at Inis mhòr
events.body: At the Seann Skell muster Buidheann an t-Seabhaig Luaidhe hears that the townsfolk of Inis mhòr fired their own coal stacks rather than let a ship of A' Chompanaidh carry them off to burn against another Seann Toll, and that the ships put in at Ros dhomhain and burned their own stores instead.

events.title: Coinneach Beag stands his first watch
events.body: By midsummer Coinneach Beag stands watch on the road north of Ros bheag with a rifle he has not yet fired, still turning over the forty-one riders and what road Strake judged worth watching instead, while the war's lines hold unmoved from where the first winter left them.

events.title: Eilidh Hale will not choose
events.body: Asked on the steps of the council hall at Baile dhìreach which people she is, Eilidh Hale, who has kept the joint council's books three winters running, answers only that she keeps the books, and no more. She is neither pressed further nor turned away, and stays in the town through the rest of the war.

events.title: Hannah Webb walks north
events.body: Hannah Webb, who keeps her vigil behind Baile chrom and nursed at Cathair gheal through the fever, walks out to meet the columns at the concession's southern edge and walks back north with them, an old woman of the last families out of Cuan shean on her arm who will not be carried.

events.title: The keys given up at Cuan shean
events.body: The harbour officers of Ceann mhòr, Cathair gheal and Inis àrsaidh ride two days south with their towns' chests of harbour keys and set them at Strake's feet on the quay at Cuan shean before his ship sails, saying only that the accounts are even and that who wants the keys after is not theirs to decide. Strake takes the chests aboard with him.

events.title: The sealed letter kept close
events.body: The last ship from over the sea puts a single sealed letter ashore for An t-Àrd-mhaor at Ros bheag before filling her berths with passengers and standing out again. Strake reads it alone by a window over the harbour, burns its wrapping in the grate, and is seen to carry the letter itself inside his coat for the rest of the winter. No clerk of his ever claims to have read a word of it.

events.title: Two scribes, one truce
events.body: At the meeting-house of Àth àrsaidh, envoys of Comhairle na Coille and of Riaghaltas nan Coigreach set down the truce of the withdrawal in two hands at once, neither side trusting the other's clerk alone with the writing of it. Three days of argument over the line on the map are settled in less than an hour once the terms are agreed.

events.title: A name given at Àth leathan
events.body: Camped a last night before the north country, several of the marching humans ask the custodians of Àth leathan the name of the place and write it down for themselves. A child born that same night under a hedge by lantern-light is given the name as though it were a christening name, none other yet being settled on her.

events.title: The keeper watches her out of sight
events.body: From the gallery of Taigh-solais Baile chrom, Lachlann mac Uisdein watches Lionel Strake's ship stand out north-about past the headland at evening, showing one light at her stern until the dark of sea and sky close over it. He writes the passing into his father's daybook in his father's own words for a night with no ship left to come.

events.title: Cha tàinig long
events.body: Fàinne nan Teintean-rabhaidh burn again from Baile chrom to Tobar dhearg, relit by the council's order, but for nothing that comes. The keepers go on filling their daybooks through the winter, oil and wind and a line where a ship would once have stood, until most of them stop troubling to leave the line at all and simply write the three words that were once Uisdean mac Lachlainn's alone.
